items.title: Danny Kelly obituary
items.summary:
Ebullient journalist, magazine editor and broadcaster whose passion for music and football shone through all his work

Danny Kelly, who has died aged 69, influenced music journalism and sports broadcasting for more than four decades. Humour, enthusiasm and encyclopedic knowledge were the hallmarks of his work as a writer and editor at the New Musical Express (NME) and Q magazine, and throughout his online, TV and audio career, most prominently around his passion for football.

In 1997 Kelly helped set up Football 365, one of the earliest football websites, and still one of the most popular in the UK. He hosted radio shows on BBC 5 Live, TalkSport, BT Sport and Times Radio, as well as many podcasts including The View from the Lane, about the team he had supported since childhood, Tottenham Hotspur.

Continue reading...
items.t: Danny Kelly obituary

items.title: Wayne Rooney says he contemplated taking own life during playing career
items.summary:
• Former England footballer opens up on mental health

  • ‘It was probably the lowest point’ at Manchester United

Wayne Rooney has revealed there was a period in his Manchester United career where he contemplated taking his own life. The former England striker said that, even as he flourished on the pitch, he was struggling with his mental health off it, despite being newly married and a dad to his eldest child, Kai.

He said he would spend two days at a time drinking at home and, he told the Life At The Midpoint with Gabby Logan podcast, at his lowest point considered taking his own life. “I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with,” Rooney said. “Then I didn’t want Kai seeing me like that, so that’s why I’d hide away as well.

items.title: Rassie Erasmus’s tired ref-blaming act is wearing thin – South Africa deserve better | Robert Kitson
items.summary:
Springboks’ achievements are remarkable but their head coach lacks statesmanship, diplomacy and good grace in defeat

So here we go again. Exactly five years have passed since South Africa’s head coach, Rassie Erasmus, first felt the full force of World Rugby’s ire for criticising match officials. And guess what? This most habitual of offenders has just copped another lengthy ban – and deservedly so – for his latest intemperate comments, notable as ever for their total lack of statesmanship, diplomacy or good grace in defeat.

To his acolytes his outspoken nature is part of what makes Rassie such a groot leier (great leader). To many others it simply cements his status as a serial prat. For the avoidance of any doubt everyone respects the remarkable achievements both of Erasmus and his double World Cup-winning teams. It is the rest of the package, sadly, that is too often a major letdown.

items.title: Pocognoli’s aspiration for how Scotland must play is in danger of becoming unworkable | Ewan Murray
items.summary:
The 4-0 debacle against Switzerland has added to the tactical concerns about the head coach’s suitability, just six games into the job

The Scottish Football Association can only cling to a lesson from the past when assessing a worrying international window. Steve Clarke was beleaguered during his early games in charge. Successive 4-0 defeats by Belgium and Russia in 2019 left Clarke with the sense he should have stayed in club management. A revival meant Clarke led his country to three out of four tournaments.

There are, however, fundamental differences between the story of Clarke and that being delivered by Sébastien Pocognoli. Clarke was a pragmatist, whose decades in coaching suggested he had the wherewithal to revive Scotland. Pocognoli, six games into his tenure, is in danger of lurching into the territory of dreamy ideologue whose aspiration for how Scotland must play is unworkable. The meek nature of Scotland’s collapse in the 4-0 loss to a second-string Switzerland was lamentable. The Belgian’s assessment, with overpraise a key theme, raised eyebrows.

items.title: Reliving the drama: England and Argentina stars watch 1986 classic with fresh eyes
items.summary:
A new film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation

“Is there anything new to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina. Flora told an audience at the London film festival premiere of the film that she played her best card then and showed Lineker an image of Maradona with Queen in 1981, during the band’s tour of Argentina. Maradona wearing a union jack T-shirt and Freddie Mercury an Argentina strip. It worked. Lineker said yes.

The rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based. The directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco play with the timeline, hopping between past and present across 91 minutes, the exact duration of the match itself. Anecdotes that now form part of Argentina’s football folklore are spliced with excellent archive material.

items.t: Reliving the drama: England and Argentina stars watch 1986 classic with fresh eyes

items.title: Bryson DeChambeau adds star quality to DP World Tour after demise of LIV Golf
items.summary:
• Player in ‘category one’ status after US Open win

  • Golfer ineligible for PGA Tour due to blanket ban

Bryson DeChambeau will add star quality to the DP World Tour next season after it was confirmed the two-time major winner has joined the circuit following the demise of LIV Golf. DeChambeau heads a list of high-profile names who will perform regularly in Europe in 2027 following LIV’s bankruptcy.

Intrigue had surrounded DeChambeau’s future. As a poster boy for LIV and its Saudi Arabian-backed disruption scheme, he appeared unwilling to feature again on traditional tours. Yet it became increasingly clear what limited options he had. The PGA Tour has been unwilling to offer an easy pathway for DeChambeau, who in theory can now play his way back there via performances in Europe. Cards will be available on the PGA Tour for 2028 through DP World Tour rankings. DeChambeau has become increasingly keen on content creation, which fuelled speculation he may skip mainstream competition entirely.

items.title: The NFL’s Salute to Service honors the military – and leaves out the realities of war | Lee Escobedo
items.summary:
This month, the league rightly honors veterans across the US. But little is mentioned about the death tolls, or the reasons behind our wars

My mom taught me to thank veterans. Whenever we saw someone in a veterans hat, she set the example. Nobody in her family served, but my paternal grandfather fought in the Pacific in the second world war, and she was always grateful to hear his stories, even the repeats.

It’s one of the things she gave me that I held on to, even in my worst years. The anger I’ve carried about the unjust wars of my lifetime – Afghanistan, Iraq and now Iran – never targeted the people sent to fight them.

items.title: Why Jordan Cox refuses to take a breather: ‘If England want me, I’ll be there’
items.summary:
Wicketkeeper-batter could have represented Australia but was destined to play for his country of birth after watching the 2010-11 Ashes at 10

In an era of sardine tin schedules and franchise teams hoping to turn heads, it was refreshing to hear Jordan Cox at the beautiful Bellerive Oval and state how desperate he is to play for England as much as is humanly possible.

When the squads for this Australia tour were being discussed, the selector Marcus North gave the wicketkeeper-batter the option to sit out the Twenty20 leg before taking on South Africa’s imposing Test attack next month. Cox, recently handed a two-year central contract after a breakout summer, was having none of it.

items.title: The Breakdown | Rattled All Blacks face rare twin threat as England eye back-to-back scalps
items.summary:
After their seismic defeat by Wales, New Zealand face the prospect of history repeating itself in unwanted ways

They still talk about the last – and only – time the All Blacks contrived to lose twice in succession to England. Back in 2002-03, as now, there was a Rugby World Cup looming in Australia and New Zealand had no shortage of quality players. “There is so much talent in New Zealand that, if they don’t win the World Cup, there should be an inquiry,” opined Steve Hansen, Wales’s head coach at the time, before England’s fateful visit to Wellington in the summer of 2003.

There’s a fresh inquiry under way now, even before the All Blacks trot out of the Twickenham tunnel this Saturday for the 48th meeting between the two nations. While Saturday’s 35-28 defeat ended a 73-year wait for a Wales win, from a home perspective it has inevitably precipitated plenty of dark muttering back in the land of the long flat white.

Continue reading...
items.t: The Breakdown | Rattled All Blacks face rare twin threat as England eye back-to-back scalps

items.title: ‘He wants to change lives’: the story behind Bukayo Saka’s Sócrates award
items.summary:
By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience

Valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue in 2022, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria. “I remember thinking: ‘Is this really Bukayo writing us an email?’” says the president of BigShoe, a non-profit organisation based in Frankfurt that has helped more than 10,000 children worldwide. “But that’s how he is. He’s always asking what more we can do.”

Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work. She got the words from Byiringiro, a 14-year-old from Rwanda who had his eyesight restored after having surgery thanks to a BigShoe initiative.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘He wants to change lives’: the story behind Bukayo Saka’s Sócrates award

items.title: Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta
items.summary:
Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead

Thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”.

Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It said he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head.

Continue reading...
items.t: Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta

items.title: I built a reputation as a ‘walker’ so I could cheat when it mattered most – and it worked | The Secret Cricket Coach
items.summary:
Cricket always celebrates sportsmanship and condemns cheating, but where exactly is the line between the two?

I once played in a one-day semi-final. We were in a very tight spot when I edged the ball to the keeper. I didn’t walk. The opposition couldn’t believe it. They crowded around me, furious, and I was getting plenty of abuse.

I managed to get a single and when I reached the other end the umpire said: “You didn’t nick that did you? You are a walker.” “Yep, that’s right,” I replied.

items.t: I built a reputation as a ‘walker’ so I could cheat when it mattered most – and it worked | The Secret Cricket Coach
